overview: Cherokee history extends beyond European written records. The Cherokee Nation rebuilt governmental and cultural institutions after forced removal, while Cherokee cultural life varies among families and communities.

items.text: The Nation adopted a written constitution in 1827 and a new constitution in 1839 after removal.
The Cherokee Advocate began publication in Tahlequah in 1844, using English and Cherokee in Sequoyah's syllabary.
In Tahlequah, Cherokee people established schools, homes, businesses and government buildings.
Language, food, storytelling and art sustain Cherokee identity. The Nation emphasizes differences among families, places and spiritual traditions.
United States troops forcibly removed Cherokee people in 1838. Survivors joined earlier western migrants and rebuilt the Nation; removal did not end Cherokee existence.
